working_title: Footprints Led to the Farm — None Led Away
alt_title: Someone Lived in Their Attic for Days
subject: Hinterkaifeck farmstead, Bavaria, 1922: the six residents were killed on the evening of 31 March and found on 4 April. Neighbours later recalled the farmer, Andreas Gruber, reporting footprints in the snow leading from the woods to the farm (ending at the barn) and none leading away, footsteps in the attic, an unfamiliar newspaper, and missing house keys. The previous maid had quit; the new maid started work the very day of the killings. In the following days visitors saw chimney smoke and the livestock had been fed: the perpetrator apparently stayed. Unsolved; 100+ suspects questioned (latest 1986).
why_potential: MrBallen 4.5M + Thoughty2 872K show demand; the footprints-in-snow image is uniquely chilling yet non-graphic; the pre-crime 'warnings' form a natural escalating evidence cadence. subject: Otzi the Iceman, found 19 Sep 1991 on the Similaun glacier, Otztal Alps (Italian-Austrian border), by German hikers Erika and Helmut Simon; ~5,300 years old. working_title: Fake Names, Wigs and a Code — Who Was She?
alt_title: Norway's Isdal Woman
subject: Isdal Woman, found 29 Nov 1970 in Isdalen near Bergen, Norway (a valley nicknamed 'Dodsdalen'/'Death Valley' for historic suicides). working_title: A Newsboy Dropped a Nickel. It Split in Half.
alt_title: The Coin That Exposed a Soviet Spy
subject: FBI 'Hollow Nickel' case: on 22 June 1953 Jimmy Bozart, 14, collecting for the Brooklyn Eagle, dropped a too-light nickel that split open to reveal microfilm of five-digit number groups. FBI cryptanalysts could not break it until Soviet agent Reino Hayhanen defected via the US embassy in Paris in 1957; the message turned out to be an innocuous 'welcome to New York' note to Hayhanen. His information led to 'Rudolf Abel' (real name William August Fisher), convicted 25 Oct 1957 and exchanged for U-2 pilot Francis Gary Powers in 1962.

working_title: The Boy Who Came From a Dark Cell
alt_title: Kaspar Hauser: 190 Years, Three DNA Tests
subject: Kaspar Hauser appeared in Nuremberg on 26 May 1828 carrying letters (one addressed to a cavalry captain), later claiming he had been kept alone in a dark cell. On 14 Dec 1833 he was stabbed in the Ansbach Hofgarten, saying a stranger lured him there and handed him a purse; the purse held a pencilled note in mirror writing. He died 17 Dec 1833. A 'lost prince of Baden' theory persisted; earlier DNA tests (1996, early 2000s) conflicted.
